sweep_summary: this search of works with stress in the title for Galela (gale1259) turned up only two title hits, and they are one work: Shelden's 'Galela phonemes and stress' (WILC 7, 1989, pp. 77-88; Glottolog 111944) and the CLDF/StressTyp2-derived duplicate record 686214 that mis-dates it as '1990, vol. 8' (the held WILC vol. 8 contains no Galela paper). This is already the catalog's deciding source and was already held held by the project as an image-only PDF plus scanned; I re-rendered and read the page scan for p. 78 and p. 85 and read the scanned of sec. 4.1-4.3: stress is on the penultimate syllable of the stem, monomorphemic words are penult, loan antepenults are analysed as underlying penult plus vowel paragogue, and 'Stress placement is not affected by affixation' (/no-tagi-kasi/, ['?umokasi]). Both items confirm the catalog's 'morphological' (stem-penult) coding; nothing new to acquire from the title search. the PDF we hold and scanned were copied into with and a note. Outside this search of works with stress in the title's item list, the only unheld corroborating sources remain van Baarda 1908 (HathiTrust full view hvd.hx4vpm, but babel.hathitrust.org still could not be reached by automated download) and the 1989 Galela conversations book (HathiTrust search-only); both are low priority and would at most corroborate Shelden.

new_statements.quote: Stress is predictable on the penultimate syllable of stems and will not be marked on words written phonemically. [p. 78] ... 4.3. Stress and affixation. Stress placement is not affected by affixation. In this respect it differs from neighboring Loloda and Tobelo (van Baarda 1904:356-9) and Tobaru (Fortgens 1928:392ff). In the following examples, the penultimate syllable of tagi is always stressed, regardless of affixes. /wo-tagi/ 'he's walking' (he-walk) /wo-tagi-li/ 'he's walking again' (he-walk-REPET) /no-tagi-kasi/ 'you walk!' (you-walk-IMPERATIVE) /wi-si-tagi-ko/ 'he's forced seawards' (him-CAUS-walk-DIR:sea) [p. 85]

new_statements.reading: Word stress is fixed on the penultimate syllable of the stem (with only apparent antepenult exceptions created by vowel paragogue on loans, which Shelden analyses as underlyingly penult); prefixes and suffixes, including the bound unstressed directional/aspectual suffixes, never attract or shift stress, e.g. ['?umokasi] for /umo-kasi/. This is a stem-domain penult system, i.e. morphologically conditioned rather than word-edge penult, which is exactly the catalog's 'morphological' coding.

new_statements.quote: [p. 356] In het Gal. hebben we gezien, dat de achterzetsels (ook de achtervoegsels: wa: niet; kawa: niet meer; li: weêr; si: nog; waàsi: nog niet; kàsi: eerst nog) geen verandering brengen in den klemtoon van 't grondwoord waarbij zij geplaatst worden. [...] Maar komen er aan de woorden in 't Lòd. achterzetsels of grammaticale achtervoegsels, dàn verspringt de klemtoon op de vòòrlaatste lettergreep van 't aldus verlengde woord. [p. 338] De toegevoegde lettergreep doet den klemtoon niet verspringen, zoodat, in de hier boven aangehaalde Lòda'sche woorden, de klemtoon steeds op de twee-na-laatste lettergreep valt.
new_statements.translation: [p. 356] In Galela we have seen that the postpositions (and also the suffixes: wa 'not'; kawa 'no longer'; li 'again'; si 'still'; waàsi 'not yet'; kàsi 'first, still') bring no change to the stress of the stem to which they are attached. [...] But when postpositions or grammatical suffixes are added to words in Loda, the stress then jumps to the penultimate syllable of the word so lengthened. [p. 338] The added syllable does not make the stress shift, so that in the Loda words cited above the stress always falls on the antepenultimate syllable.

Bijdragen tot de Taal-, Land- en Volkenkunde 56: 317-496 (the pp. 356-9 passage that Shelden 1989 cites for the Galela/Loloda stress contrast).
new_statements.locator: p. 356 (PDF spread p-21, left page, 'Waar wij hier voor 't eerst van achterzetsels spreken..'), p. 338 (PDF spread p-12, left page), p. 385 (PDF spread p-35, right page)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: p. 356 (crops/, page header '356 HET LODA'SCH, IN VERGELIJKING MET HET'): 'Waar wij hier voor 't eerst van achterzetsels spreken, is het dunkt mij hier de plaats om op te merken, dat in deze het Lod. een ingrijpend verschil vertoont met het Gal. In het Gal. hebben we gezien, dat de achterzetsels (ook de achtervoegsels: wa: niet; kawa: niet meer; li: weer; si: nog; waasi: nog niet; kasi: eerst nog) geen verandering brengen in den klemtoon van 't grondwoord waarbij zij geplaatst worden.' - verbatim on the image. Continuation (crops/, same page): 'In het Lod. krijgt men ook geen verandering in klemtoon, wanneer er aan een woord.. een verlengstuk wordt toegevoegd, zooals wij boven gezien hebben…
new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the existing Shelden 1989 statement (stem penult, unaffected by affixation) - Shelden's own citation of van Baarda 1904:356-9 for the Galela vs Loloda/Tobelo contrast is confirmed verbatim. Adds the explicit list of stress-neutral suffixes (wa, kawa, li, si, waàsi, kàsi) and the reduplication note. Catalog record itself has an empty rule field.
new_statements.rule_in_words: For Galela: word stress sits on the stem and is not moved by postpositions or by the bound suffixes wa, kawa, li, si, waàsi, kàsi (stem-domain stress). The p. 338 comparison shows the stem stress is penultimate: Galela àké, tébi, udo, ngiri correspond to Loda àkéré, tébini, ūdomo, ngiriki with the stress left in place (antepenult in Loda), and Loda words with postpositions re-stress the penult of the enlarged word, which Galela does not do.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said. p. 385 (reduplicated intensives, 'evenals in 't Gal. ook in 't Lòd.', Gal. examples da guūi-ūi, da pahàsi-hàsi, da puturu-turu, i timi-timisi): 'Het eerste lid wordt daarbij - zoo noodig - afgekort, zòò dat de klemtoon op de voorlaatste lettergreep valt' - the first member is clipped so that its stress falls on its penult, i.e. each member of the reduplication carries its own penult stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None for Galela. The Loda statements (stress shifts to the penult of the suffixed word, p. 356-357; antepenult in the lengthened cognates, p. 338) concern Loda/Loloda (loda1244), not Galela.
new_statements.identity_note: Van Baarda's data are the Galela of the Lake Galela district of northern Halmahera (missionary data, 1880s-1900s); he notes north-shore vs south-shore pronunciation differences (1895 p. 12) but none concerning stress. The 1904 work is primarily about Loda/Loloda (loda1244); only its sentences beginning 'In het Gal.' and the Galela columns of its comparisons are about Galela, and the Loda stress statements (stress shift to the penult of suffixed words; antepenult in lengthened cognates) must not be attributed to Galela.

new_statements.rule_in_words: The rule ('den regel') is stress on the penultimate syllable; the dictionary marks with a macron only the vowels stressed contrary to the rule, i.e. lexically exceptional non-penult stress exists but is the marked minority.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing on secondary stress. p. 33 (addition to § 128): in the exclamative construction ma + noun 'the noun receives a strong stress' ('Het naamwoord krijgt daarbij een sterken klemtoon'), examples ma müti 'as sweet as sugar', ma butüru 'iron-strong', ma dubüso 'as heavy as lead' - emphatic prominence, marked on the penult.
new_statements.exceptions: Implicitly: words stressed 'buiten den regel' (not penult) are macron-marked in the dictionary. One explicit case in the body (scanned text, not image-checked): the folk word nabi 'spirit of the craftsmen' with 'nadruk op den laatste[n] lettergreep' (stress on the last syllable), distinguished from Malay nabi 'prophet'. Also noted: pronunciation differs between the north and south sides of Lake Galela (p. 12), but only in segments, not stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Van Baarda's data are the Galela of the Lake Galela district of northern Halmahera (missionary data, 1880s-1900s); he notes north-shore vs south-shore pronunciation differences (1895 p. 12) but none concerning stress. The 1904 work is primarily about Loda/Loloda (loda1244); only its sentences beginning 'In het Gal.' and the Galela columns of its comparisons are about Galela, and the Loda stress statements (stress shift to the penult of suffixed words; antepenult in lengthened cognates) must not be attributed to Galela.

new_statements.quote: De klemtoon valt gewoonlijk op de voorlaatste lettergreep. „Vóór- of achtervoegsels”, lezen wij in § 5, „doen den klemtoon niet verspringen, zooals in sommige Indische talen het geval is”. Hiertegen is op te merken dat in geen enkele Indische taal de voorvoegsels invloed op den klemtoon uitoefenen en dat het bestaan van achtervoegsels in het Galelareesch, ten minste in den tegenwoordigen toestand der taal, aan twijfel onderhevig is. Wat de Schrijver voor achtervoegsels houdt, zijn achtergevoegde partikels, zooals wij later zien zullen
new_statements.translation: The stress usually falls on the penultimate syllable. 'Prefixes or suffixes', we read in par. 5 [of van Baarda's grammar], 'do not make the stress shift, as is the case in some Indonesian languages'. Against this it should be remarked that in no Indonesian language do the prefixes influence the stress, and that the existence of suffixes in Galela, at least in the present state of the language, is open to doubt. What the author takes for suffixes are postposed particles, as we shall see later.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement and same type as the catalog record (Shelden 1989: penult of the stem, unaffected by affixation, coded 'morphological') and as the existing van Baarda 1904 p. 356 statement (Galela postpositions/suffixes wa, kawa, li, si, waasi, kasi do not change the stress of the grondwoord) and the 1895 Woordenlijst par. 5 correction note (penult as the rule). CAVEAT ON On the identity of the variety: the sentence read is van Baarda's 1891 Beknopte spraakkunst par. 5 via Kern's verbatim quotation, not the 1908 Leiddraad, which remains unread; the Leiddraad is the same author's later teaching grammar of the same dialect and Shelden 1989 cites van Baarda for exactly this affix-neutral penult…
new_statements.rule_in_words: van Baarda (1891 par. 5, as quoted by Kern): word stress falls as a rule on the penultimate syllable, and adding prefixes or suffixes does not move it, i.e. stress stays on the penult of the base word (grondwoord) whatever is attached; Kern accepts the penult rule and only disputes the morphology (the 'suffixes' are postposed particles, which equally leave the base's stress untouched). This is the stem-penult, affix-neutral pattern the catalog codes as 'morphological'.
new_statements.exceptions: 'gewoonlijk' (usually) penult, no exceptions listed in the quoted passage; Kern p. 497 (same page, above) notes loanwords not adapted to native pronunciation as the locus of irregularities in sound shape; p. 525 lists the reciprocal prefix variants makoku/makoka/makoko/makokě differing in the last syllable (not a stress statement).
new_statements.identity_note: Galela ('t Galela'sch dialekt / Galelareesch / Galillareesch) of north Halmahera as described by the missionary M. J. van Baarda; Kern 1891 reviews van Baarda's 1891 Beknopte spraakkunst van de Galillareesche taal. The listed 1908 Leiddraad (same author, same dialect) itself remains unread: its only scans (Google Books Z4hAAAAAYAAJ = HathiTrust hvd.hx4vpm) are could not be reached by automated download.

sources.note: Stress is on the penultimate syllable of the STEM; monomorphemic words have penult stress; loans with vowel paragogue show surface antepenult stress but are underlyingly penult (Penultimate Stress Rule ordered before the two paragogue rules, sec. 4.1-4.2); affixation (prefixes and suffixes, including directional and aspectual suffixes, note 9: 'phonologically bound, unstressed, and inseparable') does not move stress, so stress is stem-penult, not word-penult. This is the catalog's deciding source and the passages the catalog quotes are present verbatim on the page scan.
